requirements.requirement: node1 gets a routed interface inside each VLAN (one per subnet, toward node2 and toward node3)
requirements.summary: node1 eth1 assigned 192.168.10.1/24 (toward node2's subnet) and eth2 assigned 192.168.20.1/24 (toward node3's subnet), both shown UP with the correct addresses, and confirmed still present/UP after node1's reboot.

requirements.requirement: node1 forwards IPv4 traffic between the two VLAN interfaces
requirements.summary: Global and per-interface ip_forward/forwarding sysctls set to 1 on node1, and forwarding is directly confirmed functional by cross-VLAN pings showing ttl=63 (one router hop) between node2 and node3, both before and after node1's reboot.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 (each on their own VLAN/subnet) can reach each other across the VLAN boundary via node1
requirements.summary: node2 (192.168.10.2/24) and node3 (192.168.20.2/24) were each given a static route to the other's subnet via node1, and bidirectional ping succeeded end-to-end with ttl=63, confirming a routed (not direct L2) path through node1. Connectivity was reverified after all three nodes were individually restarted.

requirements.requirement: Configuration is durable/persistent (not just runtime-only ip/nmcli state)
requirements.summary: node1's interface addresses and forwarding sysctls were written to /etc/network/interfaces.d/vlan-routing.conf and /etc/sysctl.d/99-antrieb.conf; node2/node3 addressing and routes were persisted via nmcli connection profiles. This was independently confirmed by a real reboot on all three nodes after which addresses, forwarding, routes, and cross-VLAN ping all recovered without manual reapplication.

overall_summary: The executor built a correct routed topology on node1 (two subnetted, forwarding-enabled interfaces) and demonstrated genuine cross-VLAN reachability between node2 and node3 via ttl-consistent pings, both before and after persisting the configuration through real reboots of all three nodes. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was completed for every managed node with clear boot-id transitions and full state recovery. Hygiene is good; the only blemish is an unremoved /tmp/reboot.log left by the reboot helper on node2/node3, which is bounded and low-risk.
limitations: Lifecycle after_prepare is an alias of before_prepare (prepare disabled), so all observed changes are attributable to the executor by construction; this is expected given the task configuration and not evidence of any gap.

Boot-id polling produced several transient connection-reset/timeout entries during each reboot window; these are expected artifacts of the node being offline mid-reboot and were correctly not treated as failures.

operational_hygiene.summary: Chronological review of state-changing executor commands shows each mutation maps to a material outcome or a necessary prerequisite: cmd-cb28dfaa410e47ee's flush of docker0/interfaces-config/networking.service/dhclient on node1 was needed to stop SONiC's interface reconciler from reverting the manual eth1/eth2 assignment, and the subsequent IP/route/sysctl commands on all three nodes directly implement the routing requirement. The three native reboots (cmd-2099c31ca14b40f5, cmd-80702735044e4a35, cmd-49dba734dd6f4008) are the independent restart-evidence protocol, executed sequentially with clear pre/post boot_id capture and recovery verification; the many failed/timeout boot_id polls immediately surrounding each reboot are expected transient connection loss during reboot, not unnecessary mutations. No troubleshooting experiments or unrelated mutations were found. Minor residue: the reboot helper left /tmp/reboot.log on node2 and node3, a small, low-risk, unremoved artifact rather than a reverted one.
